t: ROS 2: What ROS 2 Is: Plumbing for Robots
title: ROS 2: What ROS 2 Is: Plumbing for Robots
description: ROS 2 is the middleware that robots are built on: instead of one giant program, a robot is dozens of nodes — a lidar driver, a localizer, a planner, a motor controller — communicating over typed topics, services, and actions. Underneath is DDS (Data Distribution Service), an industrial pub/sub standard with real-time quality-of-service policies. ROS 2 adds what ROS 1 lacked: security (SROS2), lifecycle management, and real-time support. If a robot has more than one sensor and one actuator, it probably runs ROS 2.

t: ROS 2: Topics, Services, Actions: The Three Patterns
title: ROS 2: Topics, Services, Actions: The Three Patterns
description: ROS 2 has three communication patterns, and choosing correctly is the core design skill. Topics are many-to-many streaming data (sensor feeds, poses) with QoS-tuned delivery. Services are synchronous request/response (trigger a calibration, query a state). Actions are long-running goals with feedback and cancelation (navigate to waypoint, with progress updates and the ability to preempt). Misusing them — a service for streaming data, a topic for commands — is the classic beginner architecture bug.
key_facts: Actions: goals with feedback and cancel

t: ROS 2: DDS and QoS: Delivery Guarantees You Can Tune
title: ROS 2: DDS and QoS: Delivery Guarantees You Can Tune
description: DDS quality-of-service policies are ROS 2's superpower: reliability (best-effort vs reliable), durability (late joiners get history), deadline, liveliness, and history depth — per topic, per connection. A video feed uses best-effort; a stop command uses reliable with a deadline. The compatibility check is automatic: a publisher and subscriber with incompatible QoS simply do not connect, and ROS 2 tells you why. For defense networks with lossy links, QoS tuning is the difference between a robot that works and one that freezes.

t: ROS 2: SROS2: Security Built Into the Middleware
title: ROS 2: SROS2: Security Built Into the Middleware
description: SROS2 brings PKI security to the robot's nervous system: each node gets a certificate, DDS encrypts and authenticates traffic, and access-control policies declare which node may publish or subscribe to which topic. A compromised camera node cannot spoof lidar data because the policy forbids it from publishing /scan. Key management is the operational cost — but for fielded robots, an unauthenticated middleware bus is an unacceptable attack surface, and SROS2 closes it.
key_facts: Compromised nodes cannot spoof other sensors

t: ROS 2: Your First Robot: Talker, Listener, Launch
title: ROS 2: Your First Robot: Talker, Listener, Launch
description: The hello-world is the talker/listener pair: one node publishing strings on /chatter, another subscribing, both described in a launch file that starts the system with parameters. From there the ladder is parameters (runtime-tunable), then a real sensor driver, then the navigation stack. The launch system — Python-based, composable, with lifecycle hooks — is how a 40-node robot becomes one deployable instead of 40 terminal windows.
key_facts: Swarm file: one file, whole robot

t: ROS 2: Lifecycle Nodes: Managed Startup and Shutdown
title: ROS 2: Lifecycle Nodes: Managed Startup and Shutdown
description: Real robots cannot just be killed -9: sensors need ordered startup, and shutdown must park actuators safely. ROS 2 lifecycle nodes move through states — unconfigured, inactive, active, shutting down — with transitions the launch system orchestrates. A motor controller configures hardware, activates only when the planner is ready, and deactivates to a safe state on fault. This is the difference between a demo and a machine you trust near people.

title: ROS 2: Nav2: The Navigation Stack
description: Nav2 is ROS 2's navigation system: global planners (A*, Dijkstra) for the route, local planners (DWB, MPPI) for dodging, costmaps fusing lidar and cameras into obstacle grids, and behavior trees orchestrating recovery (back up, spin, replan). It navigates warehouses, campuses, and test ranges daily. Tuning costmaps and planners for the vehicle's dynamics is the real work — the defaults drive a TurtleBot, not your platform.

t: ROS 2: Defensive Uses: Uncrewed Ground Patrol
title: ROS 2: Defensive Uses: Uncrewed Ground Patrol
description: ROS 2's defensive applications are uncrewed systems doing dull, dangerous work: perimeter patrol UGVs running Nav2 with SROS2-secured comms, EOD-assist manipulators with lifecycle-managed arms, and sensor-mule robots logging infrastructure health. The common thread is the operator at a safe distance and the robot in harm's way — with the middleware's security and lifecycle guarantees making the system trustworthy enough to field.

title: ROS 2: Real-Time: Deterministic Execution
description: Some robots have hard deadlines — a 1 kHz control loop cannot wait for a garbage collector. ROS 2's real-time story is executors with deterministic scheduling, zero-copy intra-process messaging, and compatibility with real-time Linux (PREEMPT_RT) and DDS implementations tuned for determinism. The discipline is end-to-end: real-time executor, locked memory, isolated CPUs, measured worst-case latency. Soft real-time gets you smooth demos; hard real-time gets you certifiable machines.

t: ROS 2: Debugging: rqt, rosbag, and the Graph
title: ROS 2: Debugging: rqt, rosbag, and the Graph
description: ROS 2 debugging is graph debugging: rqt_graph shows the node/topic topology, ros2 topic echo shows the data, and rosbag records everything for replay — the flight-data recorder of robotics. When the robot misbehaves, you replay the bag and watch the exact messages that led to the failure. The discipline is recording always in the field: storage is cheap, and the one incident you did not record is the one you cannot diagnose.

title: ROS 2: Simulation: Gazebo Before Hardware
description: Nobody tests navigation on the real robot first: ROS 2 pairs with Gazebo (next topic's subject) for physics-accurate simulation, with rosbag bridging sim and reality. The workflow is simulate, then hardware-in-the-loop, then field — each stage catching the bugs the previous one cannot. Sensor plugins publish the same topics as real drivers, so the autonomy stack cannot tell sim from reality, which is exactly the point.

title: ROS 2: Multi-Robot: Fleets and Namespaces
description: One robot is a product; ten are a system. ROS 2 namespaces let identical software run on many robots without topic collisions (/robot3/scan), and DDS discovery scales to fleets on a shared network. Fleet managers assign tasks, monitor health, and coordinate — with SROS2 keeping each robot's bus authenticated. The hard problems are shared world models and communication dropouts, not the plumbing.

t: ROS 2: Testing: Integration Rigs and CI
title: ROS 2: Testing: Integration Rigs and CI
description: ROS 2 testing layers: unit tests per node, integration tests with the real middleware (launch_testing spins up nodes and asserts on topics), and nightly sim runs of full missions. The launch_testing framework is the workhorse — it catches the QoS mismatches and lifecycle ordering bugs that unit tests cannot. For fielded robots, the sim nightly is the gate: green sim, then hardware.
key_facts: Nightly mission sims as the gate

t: ROS 2: Real-World Pattern: Warehouse Inventory Fleet
title: ROS 2: Real-World Pattern: Warehouse Inventory Fleet
description: A complete pattern: a fleet of AMRs running Nav2, each namespaced, SROS2-secured, recording to black boxes, coordinated by a dispatcher assigning inventory-scan tasks. The robots share a world model of shelf locations; the dispatcher reassigns on battery or fault. One operator supervises twelve robots. The same architecture, with different payloads, patrols perimeters — the middleware does not care what the robot carries.
